papers.title: Parallel Teleportation via AME(5,2) States on IBM Quantum Hardware
papers.summary: The five-qubit Absolutely Maximally Entangled AME$(5,2)$ state, whose every pair of qubits is maximally mixed so that all its information lives in non-local correlations, could in principle serve as a single shared quantum networking resource for teleporting two unknown qubits in parallel (each via its own Bell measurement and Pauli correction). Nonetheless, its hardware implementations remain scarce despite its theoretical importance. Here, we demonstrate parallel teleportation based on a five-qubit absolutely maximally entangled state, AME$(5,2)$, on the superconducting processor ibm_pittsburgh. We construct three-qubit Clifford decoders that extract two Bell pairs using three logical two-qubit gates for each of 60 inequivalent sender-receiver assignments. Using parallelization and classical Pauli frame post-processing, we retain reference-receiver entanglement on both channels after three teleportation rounds. With XY4 dynamical decoupling and the lowest-cost decoder, the final entanglement fidelities are $0.704\pm0.028$ and $0.680\pm0.022$, where uncertainties are pointwise $99\%$ confidence-interval half-widths over eight trials. Their lower bounds exceed the separability threshold of $1/2$. The decoder with lower circuit depth generally retains higher mean fidelity, and XY4 generally improves on XX. These results establish a hardware demonstration of two-channel entanglement transmission through repeated AME-assisted teleportation and provide compact decoding circuits for reconfigurable multipartite communication.

papers.title: Structured light for addressable two-qubit gates in medium-sized ion crystals: modeling motional and dephasing errors
papers.summary: Geometric phase gates with addressed laser radiation are widely used in trapped-ion quantum computers to drive high-fidelity entangling gates on an arbitrary qubit pair of a larger ion chain. Such programmable connectivity exploits the collective phonons to mediate the desired interaction, while simultaneously achieving robustness to their thermal fluctuations by a careful calibration of the gate time with respect to the laser and vibrational-mode frequencies. Crosstalk errors can arise when the spectator qubits, which should ideally remain idle during the gate, are partially driven by the laser fields. The minimal crosstalk, which is set by the laser beam size on the spectator ions, can be achieved when the addressing beams propagate perpendicular to the ion chain. However, this results in exciting the radial phonons, and can complicate achieving high-fidelities as the ion chain grows due to the so-called spectral mode crowding. In this work, we present the theoretical description of a scheme recently implemented by Faorlin et $al.$. This scheme overcomes these complications by engineering addressable state-dependent forces along the ion-chain with laser beams that propagate perpendicular to it through the use of structured light gradients. In this way, one can excite the axial phonons and avoid the spectral mode crowding, while simultaneously minimizing the crosstalk. We present a detailed derivation of the entangling gate scheme, together with analytical closed-form expressions for the leading contribution to the gate error caused by thermal motional fluctuations and dephasing noise. Our results confirm that such fluctuations account for up to 93$\%$ of the error budget under the operating conditions of the gate implemented by Faorlin et $al.$. We identify target parameters to reduce the motional error from the reported $10^{-3}$ to the $10^{-5}$ level.

papers.title: Dynamical Mean-Field Theory for Real Materials using Variational Quantum Compressed Time Evolution on a Quantum Computer
papers.summary: We design a hybrid quantum-classical computational workflow, combining density functional theory and dynamical mean-field theory, to investigate the electronic properties of CaCuO2, a parent structure of high-temperature cuprate superconductors. Our approach uses a quantum algorithm as an impurity solver that is based on variational quantum compressed time evolution to compute the time-dependent Greens function on an IBM Heron quantum device. Utilizing error mitigation techniques and a Lehmann representation fitting procedure, we extract the density of states from the signal in the accessible time regime. Despite the significant challenges rooted in the residual imprecision of currently accessible NISQ devices, we successfully resolve the characteristic features of the spectral function. However, we find that the required numerical accuracy for full DMFT self-consistency exceeds current hardware capabilities, indicating that practical real-material DMFT applications will necessitate post-NISQ hardware developments.

papers.title: Observable-Level Framework for Finite-Key Security in Coherent-One-Way Quantum Key Distribution
papers.summary: Practical security analysis of Coherent-One-Way (COW) quantum key distribution requires optical-device modeling, finite experimental statistics, and security inference to be treated consistently without conflating assumptions. We present a modular observable-level simulation framework organized through the pipeline {\theta}_phys -> p -> O -> S_j(O), in which physical source, channel, receiver, and detector parameters determine detector-resolved event probabilities, a finite-block layer applies an effective dead-time treatment and generates aggregate detector counts, and interchangeable security evaluators act on the same observable record. The framework is verified against analytical optical, virtual-state, and finite-key relations and evaluated against reported experimental COW-QKD operating points. The Kato finite-key calculation reproduces the refined experimentally reported secure-key rates most closely at intermediate distances, with deviations of -1.5% at 50 km and -10.3% at 75 km. Monitoring bright-port decoy counts agree within 0.9-2.4%, while remaining distance-dependent dark-port residual identifies the principal model-sensitive observable of the present physical description. Applying Kato and Azuma-Hoeffding concentration treatments to identical detector records isolates the effect of finite-key statistical inference and shows substantially tighter Kato phase-error bounds for rare-event monitoring records studied here. Holding the Kato evaluator fixed, joint optimization of coherent-state mean photon number mu and receiver splitting fraction t_B increases model-predicted secure-key rate by 7.4-20.2% relative to optimization of mu alone with t_B = 0.3. The framework therefore provides a common computational interface for experimental reproduction, controlled security-model comparison, model-based protocol optimization, and modular adversarial stress testing in COW-QKD.

papers.title: Ensemble basis-free coherence for quantum communication
papers.summary: The resource theory of coherence quantifies the quantum properties of states and their role in quantum information processing. Extending coherence theory to ensembles, the natural objects in quantum communication, remains an active research direction, with their operational potential still being explored. In this work, we establish a maximally coherent ensemble in every finite dimension: the continuous ensemble of pure states distributed according to the normalized Haar measure attains the tight upper bound on basis-free relative entropy ensemble coherence. We then prove that ensemble coherence bounds the effective informational advantage of postselective measurements over the Holevo quantity for two equiprobable pure states. Finally, for the qubit B92 QKD protocol, we show that the coherence of Alice's ensemble upper-bounds the secret key rate in the asymptotic regime. These results give ensemble coherence a quantitative operational meaning in quantum communication and cryptography

papers.title: Floquet ground state order
papers.summary: Clean, interacting, periodically driven systems are believed to thermalize to featureless, infinite-temperature states that preclude the formation of stable ordered states. Here, we show stable quantum order, distinct from prethermal order, and its phase transitions in the ground state of the average-energy operator. Decomposing the time evolution into geometric and average-energy dynamics, we apply Geometric Floquet theory to identify the Floquet ground state. We derive a general variational principle to compute the Floquet ground state in large interacting periodically driven systems, and use it to develop a matrix product state algorithm. In driven nonintegrable chains of more than 100 interacting spins, our numerical simulations exhibit a gapped, area-law entangled Floquet ground state in extended parameter regimes; the ground-state manifold can support both dressed equilibrium order (e.g., Floquet antiferromagnets) and inherently nonequilibrium order (e.g., ground-state time crystals). This quantum order is protected by a finite average-energy gap, which closes at phase transition points upon changing model parameters. We decompose Floquet phases of matter into their equilibrium and nonequilibrium elements: whereas the Floquet ground state at any fixed time is a representative of an equilibrium phase of matter, the nonequilibrium content is entirely produced by the drive holonomy and is geometric. Finally, we identify quasilocal counterdiabatic driving as a mechanism for the stability against heating of gapped Floquet ground states in nonintegrable quantum systems, and argue why Floquet ground states evade the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis. Our work enables the study of interacting nonequilibrium matter deep into the many-body regime, and lays the foundations for the engineering of strongly correlated ordered quantum states.

papers.title: Quantum Broker: QoS-Aware Distribution of Quantum Computations
papers.summary: Cloud-accessible quantum computing has made heterogeneous Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) available through provider platforms that differ in qubit technology, calibration state, queueing behavior, and pricing model. This heterogeneity makes execution management a quantum-engineering concern: a quantum circuit may be executable on several backends, but the resulting cost, latency, fidelity, and reproducibility depend on backend selection and on how measurement shots are allocated. This paper presents the Quantum Broker, an open-source and provider-agnostic framework for Quality-of-Service-aware quantum execution management. The framework operationalizes shot-wise distribution by exploiting the statistical independence of quantum measurement shots to dispatch a single circuit across multiple heterogeneous QPUs according to user-defined constraints and optimization objectives. It combines a modular execution architecture, interchangeable backend-profiling strategies, and the Quantum QoS Specification Language (QQSpec), a declarative language for expressing QoS requirements. Dispatch planning is supported by two solver backends: a mixed-integer linear-programming (MILP) solver, and a nonlinear dual-annealing solver. Experiments on benchmark quantum circuits and noisy simulator backends show that the Quantum Broker can produce feasible QoS-aware dispatch plans under heterogeneous backend conditions and can improve QoS satisfaction with respect to single-backend and naive multi-backend baselines. The results also expose a practical trade-off between planning time and dispatch quality, with the nonlinear solver producing higher-quality allocations at increased computational cost. Overall, the Quantum Broker provides an extensible execution-management layer for engineering portable, reproducible, and QoS-aware quantum software over fragmented quantum cloud infrastructures.

papers.title: CO$\Phi$ - COmpiling PHotonics into dIgital quantum circuits
papers.summary: Photonic and qubit-based (digital) approaches to quantum computing are largely regarded as separate paradigms. This article aims to bridge these paradigms by developing a method for mapping quantum-optical systems onto qubit-based quantum circuits. The key ingredient enabling this mapping is the introduction of a truncation of the Fock space describing single-mode optical states. Within this framework, representations of basic photonic operations are developed, including the phase-rotation operator, the displacement operator, the squeezing operator, and the beam splitter. Explicit quantum circuit constructions are provided for Fock-space truncations of dimension $N=2$ and $N=4$. We discuss benchmarking of the implemented operations and identify the regime of applicability and the limitations of the proposed method. The presented results can be used to simulate quantum optical circuits on qubit-based quantum computers, with special relevance to Gaussian Boson Sampling in the low-photon-number regime. To demonstrate the practical applicability of this approach, we complement the theoretical framework with a Python-based quantum programming tool CO$\Phi$ that compiles Blackbird quantum-optics programs into qubit-based OpenQASM circuits using a truncated Fock-space encoding. The compiler is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Quantum-Cosmos-Lab/cophi.

papers.title: Capturing Open Quantum System Dynamics with Compact Dressed Hamiltonians
papers.summary: We advance the compact dressed Hamiltonian (CDH) framework to simulate the dynamics of open quantum systems strongly coupled to structured bosonic environments. The CDH approach combines reaction-coordinate mapping with a polaron transformation, incorporating strong system-environment hybridization into a dressed representation before truncating the collective bosonic mode. As a result of this truncation, dynamical features are captured with substantially fewer states than in the original representation. The residual environment is treated using a weak-coupling Markovian quantum master equation. We benchmark the method for spin-boson-type models including a single spin, coupled spins, and spin ensembles, considering both resonant and off-resonant regimes and weak to strong system-bath coupling. Comparisons with hierarchical equations of motion and converged reaction-coordinate calculations demonstrate that the CDH representation systematically approaches the reference dynamics with a compact Hilbert space, accurately reproducing oscillation frequencies, relaxation behavior, and long-time populations over a broad parameter regime. The method further captures cooperative phenomena, including bath-mediated interactions, synchronization between spins, and signatures for collective emission. Beyond efficient time propagation, the CDH framework provides direct access to the spectrum and eigenmodes of the Liouvillian. We demonstrate that slow dynamical modes converge rapidly in the CDH representation, enabling identification of relaxation timescales without fitting time-dependent observables. As a whole, the CDH framework provides an efficient and physical description of strongly coupled open quantum-system dynamics.

papers.title: Hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ over finite chain rings
papers.summary: We give a bounded-error quantum polynomial-time algorithm for finding hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ over any effectively presented finite chain ring $R$. We call auxiliary group elements or subgroups used to extract information through oracle queries \emph{probes}. For chain length at least two, elementary abelian socle probes first recover the complete flag modulo the maximal ideal. When the residue field has size $q\ge3$, we reconstruct the flag recursively, lifting rank-one terminal members one digit at a time. The intermediate digits reduce to abelian hidden subgroup problems, while the final digit is a finite-field multiple-shift problem solved using learning from subset and Fourier sampling. For $q=2$, where distinct flags can have the same stabilizer, we instead lift the conjugate parabolic subgroup through the congruence filtration. A final linear system determines it modulo normalizer directions. The algorithm outputs generators with probability at least $1-\epsilon$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log|R|,\log(1/\epsilon))$. Consequences include $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$ for every $N\ge2$ and, with an explicit maximal-order presentation, $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal{O_K}/N\mathcal{O_K})$ for number fields $K$.

papers.title: Stable charged energy and phase transitions in an anisotropic Dicke quantum battery with Kerr nonlinearity
papers.summary: Phase transitions (PTs) in quantum many-body systems offer a powerful route to manipulate the performance of quantum batteries (QBs). Here, we investigate an anisotropic Dicke QB with Kerr nonlinearity, focusing on the role of PTs in the charging process of the QB system. By analyzing how the Kerr nonlinearity reshapes the cavity level-spacing structure, we find that multiple near-degeneracies emerge at specific nonlinearity strengths. Away from the region of multiple near-degeneracies, the stable stored energy is governed primarily by the ergodic-nonergodic transition (ENET), whereas within this region it is controlled by first- and second-order dissipative phase transitions (DPTs). We employ Liouvillian spectral theory to quantify the critical slowing down associated with the DPTs, and use the Wigner function to characterize the properties of the cavity field in the vicinity of criticality. We optimize the charging process via reinforcement learning (RL) and reveal the physical mechanism underlying performance enhancement from the perspective of ergodic and nonergodic phase dynamics. Our results offer a feasible pathway for manipulating and optimizing quantum battery performance based on intrinsic PT behaviors.

papers.title: Scrambling Separates Superradiance from Quantum Chaos
papers.summary: Early studies on the Dicke model linked superradiance to quantum chaos, whereas later anisotropic Dicke and Rabi studies reached apparently conflicting conclusions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing global chaos from local instability. Along the isotropic Dicke path, a sweep at fixed low excitation energy crosses both the superradiant boundary and a nearby chaotic window, explaining the reported correlation. However, the anisotropic Dicke model can be chaotic in the normal phase and regular in the superradiant phase, making superradiance neither necessary nor sufficient for global chaos. A fidelity out-of-time-order correlator (FOTOC), in contrast, probes the local stability of the stationary point selected by the initial wave packet. The superradiant transition destabilizes the origin, whereas a change in anisotropy can restore its stability and create displaced saddles. Wave packets centered at these saddles exhibit exponential FOTOC growth even on a classically regular Dicke energy shell with Poisson statistics. This local sensitivity also enables quantitative spectroscopy: combined with the topology of stationary points and local density of states relations, FOTOC dynamics reconstructs the absolute amplitudes of spectral singularities in both models without fitting the density of states.

papers.title: Chaos and scrambling in anisotropic Dicke and Rabi models
papers.summary: Identifying the quantum signatures of classical chaos remains a central question in quantum physics, and quantum scrambling provides a new perspective on this correspondence. We study two distinct limits of the same model to examine how the correspondence between chaos and scrambling changes across different regimes. The thermodynamic-limit anisotropic Dicke model exhibits a close correspondence between chaos and scrambling, whereas this correspondence breaks down in the large-frequency-ratio limit of the anisotropic Rabi model (ARM). The contrasting chaotic behavior in the two limits originates from the different numbers of classical degrees of freedom, whereas their similar scrambling behavior stems from eigenstate delocalization. This implies that, in the large-frequency-ratio limit, eigenstate delocalization alone is insufficient to qualify the ARM as a classically chaotic model. This finding suggests that identifying chaos in quantum systems requires jointly considering the classical degrees of freedom and eigenstate delocalization.

papers.title: Quantum Simulation of the Static Yukawa Model via Effective Particles on a Trapped-Ion Quantum Simulator
papers.summary: Trapped-ion, neutral-atom, and circuit QED quantum computers naturally enable coupled qubit-boson simulations. Boson-fermion interactions arise in quantum field theory, where renormalization is required to obtain finite results. We study one of the simplest examples of a coupled fermion-boson system, the static Yukawa model, on the QSCOUT trapped-ion system. We use similarity renormalization to express the same physics in terms of effective particles described by different values of the renormalization parameter $s$. This enables us to map data taken in the window of bosonic occupancy that is experimentally accessible to larger occupancies of distinct effective particles. We use this to study strongly coupled, high-occupancy regimes despite limited readout ranges. Using a trapped-ion qubit-boson device on Sandia National Laboratories' QSCOUT platform, we demonstrate the time evolution of the static Yukawa model.

papers.title: Tuning between collective dynamics and scrambling through initial-state symmetry alignment in long-range spin models
papers.summary: Long-range interactions in many-body quantum systems give rise to a wide range of dynamical phenomena, from collective dynamics well described by integrable mean-field models with symmetric all-to-all couplings, to fast scrambling of quantum information from disordered long-range interactions. Here, we investigate scenarios in which both regimes emerge within a single deterministic, translation-invariant XY spin model with long-range couplings. We consider a sparse powers-of-two (PWR2) graph, where each spin interacts with a logarithmic number of neighbors, and a power-law-decaying model. By altering the initial state via local perturbations on a completely symmetric state, we show that the dynamics changes from collective to scrambling as witnessed by bipartite and multipartite entanglement measures. We characterize this collective-to-scrambling crossover using Lyapunov exponents in the semiclassical regime, and show that the spectral properties of the coupling graph adjacency matrix provide a very efficient tool to predict the onset of fast scrambling. Our results offer a unified framework for controlling the switch between collective and scrambling dynamics in a setup accessible in experiments with neutral atoms in cavities or in tweezer arrays.

papers.title: Efficient Ground-State Manifold Amplification for Rydberg Atom Arrays via Houdayer Cluster Updates
papers.summary: We demonstrate a hybrid quantum-classical approach for exploring ground-state manifolds of maximum independent set problems, in which quantum hardware supplies the initial solutions and an entirely classical post-processing algorithm expands them, increasing the solution diversity of quantum hardware measurements by up to several orders of magnitude. Quantum optimization devices, while capable of generating high-quality solutions, can suffer from fundamental sampling limitations. This is particularly problematic for applications that strongly depend on a large variety of uncorrelated optimal solutions. We apply the Houdayer cluster update algorithm to systematically expand quantum-generated solution sets through classical post-processing. We validate our approach on a test bed of 43 problem instances from QuEra's Aquila analog annealing device, achieving diversity amplification factors, defined as the increase in the number of distinct solutions at a given set size, of up to 11923x with a median of 24.3x across different problem scales and hardness parameters. Because exact ground-state degeneracies are known for these instances, the recovered fraction of the manifold can be measured rather than bounded: post-processing recovers a median of 21% of the ground-state manifold, and provably all of it for six instances. We also demonstrate that, in some cases, the classical post-processing can discover independent sets larger than those found by the quantum hardware, thus improving on solution quality and not just diversity. While the method is non-ergodic and cannot guarantee complete manifold coverage, it consistently discovers a larger number of high-quality, and in some cases strictly better, configurations than quantum sampling alone. This work demonstrates how simple classical post-processing can enhance the utility of quantum optimization results.

papers.title: NeST: ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes with sub-$50\mu$s stabiliser cycles via spin shuttling
papers.summary: Quantum low-density parity-check codes now reach encoding rates up to 50% at useful distances. Their checks however are long-range group actions, not local neighbourhoods, and that connectivity has so far been supplied by neutral atoms. Silicon spin qubits offer the same primitive --- coherent transport of qubit blocks --- through electron shuttling, and on microsecond rather than millisecond timescales. They however travel along fabricated tracks rather than free space: permutations an atom array obtains by moving tweezers must here become collision-free motions on a physical lattice. We here present the first code and spin-qubit hardware co-design. We build an architecture whose geometry mimics that of a family of non-abelian groups, broad enough to host codes of excellent parameters: a hierarchy of nested conveyor-belt loops on a plain square lattice of shuttling tracks, in which every group multiplication becomes a rigid, globally controlled motion of whole qubit trains. We call it NeST, for Nested Shuttling Tracks. A code search over the family returns rate-20% mitten codes up to $[[1400,280,\leq 28]]$, and circuit-level simulations including shuttling dephasing give thresholds above $10^{-3}$ with sub-$50\mu$s stabiliser cycles, two to three orders of magnitude faster than neutral-atom implementations. Via extrapolations, we estimate that this largest code may reach a logical error probability per qubit per round of $10^{-14}$, assuming a ten-fold improvement on early shuttling demonstrations, with other physical errors at p=0.1%. Logic is compatible with NeST too: for the [[150,30,10]] code we build a code-surgery gadget in which every qubit again moves only by rigid belt motions, at no qubit cost and a 29% increase in gate layers. This demonstrates that ultra-low-overhead fault tolerance and a fast clock speed are not competing goals, and that silicon spin qubits can supply both.

papers.title: Cumulative locality governs collective quantum charging
papers.summary: Quantum batteries can outperform their classical counterparts through collective quantum effects, yet the conditions enabling such advantage remain unclear. Using a generic class of free-fermionic chargers we prove that global operators are insufficient for scalable superextensive charging and that a cumulative hierarchy of many-body operators is required, with the structure of the battery determining the degree of advantage. This is obtained by relating the charging power to the norm of the commutator between the battery and charger Hamiltonians and deriving an upper bound only capturing noncommuting terms. Moreover, we revisit the concept of participation number and propose an effective definition that accounts for the relative strength of the contributing terms, correlating it with the charging power scaling. Not limited to quadratic Hamiltonians, our results establish cumulative locality as a key resource for quantum charging advantage.

papers.title: Elastic field causing noncommutativity
papers.summary: We study how a uniform torsion background, modeling a continuous density of screw dislocations and induces effective spatial noncommutativity and reshapes the energy spectrum of a free quantum particle. Within the geometric theory of defects, the metric yields a first-order (magnetic-like) coupling in the transverse dynamics, equivalent to an effective magnetic field $B_{eff}$ proportional to $p_z Omega$, where $Omega$ encodes the torsion strength. In the strong-coupling (Landau) regime, the planar coordinates obey [x,y] != 0 and the spectrum organizes into Landau-like levels with a slight electric-field-driven tilt and a uniform shift. Thus, increasing $Omega$ drives the system continuously toward the familiar Landau problem in flat space, with torsion setting the noncommutativity scale and controlling the approach to the Landau limit.

papers.title: Quantum-Seeded Distributed Post-Quantum Group Signatures for 5G V2X Communications
papers.summary: Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications rely on elliptic-curve signatures that a quantum adversary breaks and on pseudonym certificates whose anonymity rests on rotation rate, not cryptography. On a testbed with emulated 5G links, median end-to-end latency stayed within the 100ms ETSI budget for every variant. The qDGSP-EA intra-cell DENM matched the NIST ML-DSA-65 baseline on the wire, and under load EA mode raised delivery from roughly 78% to 93%.

papers.title: Orchestrating Key Scarcity: Global Capacity Allocation in Hybrid QKD-PQC Networks
papers.summary: This article presents a Distributed Key Management System (DKMS) that provisions quantum-safe symmetric encryption keys to applications across a network. To overcome the distance and rate limitations inherent to Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), the architecture adopts a hybrid design: it utilizes multi-hop trusted relays for physical key transport, while applying an end-to-end Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) layer to ensure the relayed key material remains strictly protected from intermediate nodes. Because QKD transforms key generation into a scarce physical resource, managing unpredictable application demands poses a critical capacity allocation problem. The core contribution of this work is an SDN-driven control plane that globally orchestrates the network. Rather than relying on vulnerable hop-by-hop capacity reservations, a central controller simultaneously computes optimal filling rates and multipath routing for all per-peer key buffers. This global orchestration ensures that no application is starved and that all key buffers synchronize their filling processes. Evaluated on a Kubernetes-based digital twin across five distinct network topologies, the controller successfully filled all key buffers to capacity in under six minutes. Furthermore, under deliberately excessive demand, the network demonstrated graceful degradation, safely rejecting excess requests through controlled rate-limiting rather than experiencing catastrophic failure.

papers.title: Quantum-Classical Hybrid Methods for Optimization: Lessons from Classical Decomposition
papers.summary: Quantum and physics-inspired solvers provide specialized sampling interfaces for Ising and quadratic unconstrained binary optimization models, but constrained optimization requires broader coordination and certification. This survey uses classical decomposition to analyze how such solvers can be integrated into hybrid quantum-classical algorithms. We distinguish formal decomposition, reformulation and reduction, and computational orchestration. For each interface, we ask what the transformation preserves, which assumptions make the outer method converge, and which certificates the implemented inner routine supplies. The central questions are whether that information meets the classical algorithm's requirements and whether hybridization improves solution quality or total cost enough to justify its coordination overhead. Benders decomposition, column generation, graph reduction, and copositive methods illustrate this distinction by separating heuristic proposals from classical certification. We also distinguish component effects within a fixed wrapper, reduction--solver interactions, and comparisons between complete quantum-enabled and classical systems. The analyzed studies provide conditional component benefits and favorable co-design evidence, but do not establish transferable end-to-end superiority over strong classical comparators. The resulting framework identifies opportunities for constraint programming and operations research in structure-preserving design, safeguarded hybrid algorithms, and controlled benchmarking.

papers.title: Steering of topological criticality in the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain via non-Hermitian substitutional impurities
papers.summary: We investigate the topological phase in a one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain in the presence of a finite concentration of non-Hermitian substitutional impurities. Our primary focus is the discovery of a deterministic mechanism to actively reconfigure the topological phase boundaries by introducing site-dependent, non-reciprocal intracell and intercell hopping amplitudes. Specifically, breaking the internal structural symmetry of the non-reciprocal impurity hoppings induces a targeted macroscopic displacement of the critical point. This mechanism allows for the controlled expansion or compression of the topological phase strictly via local defect asymmetry. We validate this boundary displacement through finite-size scaling analysis. The extracted correlation length critical exponents ($\nu \approx 1.455$ and $\nu \approx 1.397$ for symmetric and asymmetric configurations, respectively) confirm a disorder-induced departure from the pristine SSH universality class, with the exponent diverging at high defect densities. We also report an impurity-induced real-to-complex spectral transition geometrically characterized by the Non-Hermitian Skin Effect. Ultimately, our results establish how isolated non-Hermitian asymmetries cooperatively interact to deterministically shift macroscopic topological protection.

papers.title: Atmospheric channel model for QKD over satellite megaconstellations
papers.summary: Atmospheric turbulence and channel loss represent the primary limiting factors in ground-to-satellite quantum communication systems, yet their joint impact remains insufficiently characterized across diverse operational conditions. In this work, we develop a comprehensive and open atmospheric channel model for quantum optical links along ground-to-satellite paths, integrating altitude-dependent molecular and aerosol absorptions. The model is validated with available data from missions such as Micius and Hispasat, including a secondary viability assessment for a hypothetical Starlink-based quantum communication network, where we evaluate the predicted channel behavior in terms of single-photon transmittance and power balance, alongside the channel capacity of the link for uplink and downlink exclusively. Our comparative analysis demonstrates the ability of our channel model to predict real data under simple atmospheric behavior assumptions, which offer practical guidelines for the design and optimization of future quantum satellite missions.

papers.title: Moments of Random Permanents and Hafnians: A Replica Approach
papers.summary: Using contour-integral representations of the permanent and of the Hafnian, we turn the computation of their moments for random matrices into a replica calculation, analogous to that of the moments of the partition function of a mean-field spin glass. For the $2k$-th moment of $N\times N$ matrices with independent entries, the dominant saddle point is replica symmetric for $k>2$, and we obtain in closed form the exponential growth rate, the prefactor and the first $1/N$ correction, in agreement with exact enumerations. The growth rate depends only on whether the entries are real or complex; higher cumulants affect only the prefactor and the $1/N$ term. At $k=2$ the replica-symmetric solution becomes unstable, separating a power-law bulk of the distribution from a large-deviation tail, which we compute. The results apply to boson sampling with single photons and with squeezed light.

papers.title: Computing excited states of dipolar Bose--Einstein condensates by constrained gentlest ascent dynamics
papers.summary: Dipolar Bose--Einstein condensates (BECs), i.e., BECs with long-range dipole-dipole interactions (DDI), exhibit extraordinarily rich physics and serve as a versatile experimental platform for exploring exotic quantum states of matter. Within the mean-field framework, a dipolar BEC can be described by the Gross--Pitaevskii (GP) model with a DDI term. Its stationary states consist of the ground state, which minimizes the GP energy functional under the normalization constraint, and excited states, which are higher-energy critical points that typically correspond to constrained saddle points. Excited states encode collective excitation modes and play a key role in the dynamical stability and quantum phase transitions of cold-atom systems. However, in contrast to the extensively studied ground state, they remain far less explored numerically, especially in dipolar systems. In this work, we develop a numerical method based on the constrained gentlest ascent dynamics (CGAD) that systematically computes excited states of dipolar BECs by stably targeting constrained saddle points with any prescribed Morse index. Specifically, a semi-implicit sine-pseudospectral discretization with an orthonormalization correction step is adopted, and the nonlocal DDI terms are evaluated efficiently and accurately via the nonuniform fast Fourier transform (NUFFT). The resulting scheme is applied to one-, two-, and three-dimensional dipolar BECs, enabling a detailed numerical investigation of their excited states. Remarkably, our simulations reveal that excited states can persist even in regimes where the ground state of the condensate becomes mean-field unstable. This work provides a computational framework for studying excited states in dipolar quantum gases and offers insights for future theoretical and experimental investigations.

papers.title: Certified Non-Degenerate Maximum-Likelihood Benchmarking of Quantum LDPC Decoders
papers.summary: The measured logical error rate of a quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) code depends on the decoding algorithm. We develop a framework that certifies non-degenerate maximum-likelihood (ML) decoding outcomes on individual sampled shots under circuit-level noise, providing a common reference for comparing decoders and codes. Upper and lower bounds on the minimum correction cost in the true and competing logical classes establish success, failure, or an undecided outcome. Branch-and-bound search refines these intervals while retaining valid bounds under resource limits. Counting the outcomes bounds the empirical ML logical error rate, with interval width equal to the undecided fraction. Results for two bivariate bicycle codes show that best-first ordered statistics decoding (BF-OSD) tracks the non-degenerate ML benchmark closely while leaving some ML-correctable shots.

papers.title: Dynamics of two bosons with density-assisted tunnelling in a one-dimensional tilted lattice
papers.summary: We investigate the dynamics of two bosons in a tilted one-dimensional optical lattice with both standard and density-assisted tunnelling. The relative sign of the two tunnelling processes strongly affects the Bloch dynamics, leading to distinct reinforcing and competing regimes. We examine how the tunnelling processes generate correlations and find that, in the absence of onsite interactions, the early-time entanglement growth follows the same scaling with the density-assisted tunnelling amplitude. Finite onsite interaction changes this picture by breaking the symmetry between the reinforcing and competing regimes and enhancing the correlation differently in two regimes. This shows how the interplay between the two tunnelling mechanisms can change dyanmics and entanglement in a controlled few-body setting. Particularly, at equal tunnelling amplitudes, the doublon and singlon sectors decouple completely for arbitrary onsite interaction, lattice tilting, and initial state.

papers.title: Orbital-angular-momentum control of localized Floquet states and photocurrents in Weyl semimetals
papers.summary: Structured light provides a route to controlling quantum materials not only through its polarization, but also through its spatial profile and orbital angular momentum (OAM). We develop real space theories of a Weyl semimetal driven by a vortex beam and show that optical OAM generates highly localized Floquet vortex states with pronounced circulating photocurrents. Exploiting cylindrical symmetry, we derive a Bogoliubov-de Gennes-like radial equation that resolves the states by angular momentum and reveals their evolution between the light-dressed Weyl cones. For Laguerre-Gaussian beams, the spatially varying drive produces strong hybridization between localized vortex states and bulk states. We complement this continuum description with a Wilson-lattice formulation that retains the full two-dimensional spatial structure and enables direct calculation of local photocurrents. Both approaches consistently identify OAM-induced vortex states localized around the beam axis. The lattice calculation further shows that these states support substantially stronger circulating current densities than the more extended surface states, with the largest current densities associated with the most strongly localized, low-angular-momentum vortex modes. Our results establish optical OAM as a tunable control parameter for creating and manipulating localized current-carrying states in Weyl systems and provide a real-space framework for studying photocurrents generated by spatially structured light.

papers.title: Entanglement Distribution in Quantum Switch Networks: Memory Limits and Achievability
papers.summary: We study the minimum persistent memory required to distribute a graph state through a quantum switch. Specifically, consider a central switch that assists $n$ remote users in distributing a graph state, using independently generated user-switch Bell pairs. Since Bell-pair generation is probabilistic, different links generally succeed at different times. When a Bell-pair is generated, the qubits may need to be stored in memory while waiting for other links to succeed. Recently, new protocols have been proposed to reduce this storage overhead by processing and releasing some switch qubits before all Bell links are available. However, these protocols do not characterize the minimum persistent switch memory required at each stage. Moreover, the local-cover method in the state-of-the-art Piecemaker protocol is computationally expensive for general target graphs. In this work, we characterize the minimum persistent switch memory required after any subset of users' Bell links are generated and processed. We then develop an online stabilizer-transition protocol that attains this limit, which can be implemented in polynomial time in the number of qubits $n$. Remarkably, this optimal protocol can provide substantial memory reductions over existing heuristic approaches. In particular, for the path graph $P_n$ over $n$ users, Piecemaker protocol requires at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ qubits of peak persistent memory for \textit{every Bell-links generation order}, whereas under the order $(1,2,\ldots,n)$, our protocol requires only one persistent switch qubit. Finally, the same stabilizer-transition framework also provides a direct forward construction for sequential graph-state generation using the minimum number of quantum emitters, equal to the maximum of the height function.

papers.title: Characterizing supersolid phase transitions in trapped quantum gases with tilted dipoles at finite temperature
papers.summary: Motivated by a recent experimental work $[\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20327}{\text{arXiv:}2608.20327}]$, we theoretically investigate the nature of phase transitions in a trapped dipolar quantum gas upon tuning the contact interaction strength and dipole orientation. Using extended Gross-Pitaevskii simulations including thermal and quantum effects, we map the phase diagram comprising unmodulated superfluids, triangular droplet arrays, and stripe states. We further characterize the order of the transitions separating them through imaginary-time hysteresis analysis. The unmodulated-to-modulated transition evolves from discontinuous to continuous with increasing dipole tilt before becoming discontinuous again at large tilts. The degree of continuity is further affected by particle number, temperature, and confinement. While continuous behavior generally correlates with the emergence of stripe states, this correspondence is not systematic, and finite-size effects also influence the continuity of the transition. The triangular-to-stripe transition is found to be discontinuous at small contact interaction strengths and becomes increasingly continuous upon approaching the unmodulated-to-modulated phase boundary. Our results reveal a tunable transition order in finite dipolar quantum gases and provide guidance for its experimental investigation.

papers.title: Quantum entanglement and contextuality with complexifications of $E_8$ root system
papers.summary: The Witting configuration with 40 complex rays was suggested as a possible reformulation of Penrose model with two spin-3/2 systems based on geometry of dodecahedron and used for analysis of nonlocality and contextuality in quantum mechanics. Despite of different number of states both configurations can be derived from complexification of 240 minimal vectors of 8D real lattice corresponding to root system of Lie algebra $E_8$. An analysis of properties of suggested configuration of quantum states is provided using many analogies with properties of Witting configuration.

papers.title: Variational Perturbation Theory in Open Quantum Systems for Efficient Steady State Computation
papers.summary: Determining the steady state of an open quantum system is crucial for characterizing quantum devices and studying various physical phenomena. Often, computing a single steady state is insufficient, and it is necessary to explore its dependence on multiple external parameters. In such cases, calculating the steady state independently for each combination of parameters quickly becomes intractable. Perturbation theory (PT) can mitigate this challenge by expanding steady states around reference parameters, minimizing redundant computations across neighboring parameter values. However, PT has two significant limitations: it relies on the pseudo-inverse -- a numerically costly operation -- and has a limited radius of convergence. In this work, we remove both of these roadblocks. First, we introduce a variational perturbation theory (VPT) and its multipoint generalization that significantly extends the radius of convergence even in the presence of non-analytic effects such as dissipative phase transitions. Then, we develop two numerical strategies that eliminate the need to compute pseudo-inverses. The first relies on a single LU decomposition to efficiently construct the steady state within the convergence region, while the second reformulates VPT as a Krylov space recycling problem and uses preconditioned iterative methods. We benchmark these approaches across various models, demonstrating their broad applicability and significant improvements over standard PT.

papers.title: Correlated emission of electron-current waves
papers.summary: Correlated emission of light offers a potential avenue for entanglement generation between atomic spins, with potential application for sensing and quantum memory. In this work, we investigate the conditions for the correlated emission by color centers into an electronic bath of conduction electrons. Unlike emission into bosonic modes, electrons can absorb energy via two-particle processes across a large range of length scales. We find that two length scales are particularly relevant in a clean system: one set by the Fermi velocity and the frequency of the color centers $v_F/\Delta$, and the other set by the Fermi wavelength $\lambda_F \ll v_F/\Delta$. Subradiance requires emitters to be spaced at a distance closer than the Fermi wavelength, while superradiance requires spacing less than $\sqrt{\lambda_F v_F/\Delta}$, so long as the emitters are initialized with coherence. We show that the emitted current burst has a spiral form, and we discuss the experimental possibility to observe correlated dissipation by color-center qubits coupled to electronic environments.

papers.title: QUT: A Unit Testing Framework for Quantum Subroutines
papers.summary: We present the architectural design and prototype implementation of QUT (Quantum Unit Testing), a framework for unit testing of quantum subroutines. The framework is developed with a focus on usability and simplicity, making the complex theoretical concepts behind quantum unit testing accessible to a wide range of users with diverse backgrounds. This is achieved through the implementation of polymorphic probabilistic assertions, whose evaluation methods adapt to the data types of the arguments used in assertion statements, which may vary according to the context-dependent semantics of quantum subroutines. These arguments can be represented as qubit measurement outcomes, density matrices, or Choi matrices. For each type, the architecture integrates a specific testing protocol - such as quantum process tomography, quantum state tomography, or Pearson's chi-squared test - while remaining flexible enough to incorporate additional protocols in the future. The framework is built on the Qiskit software stack, providing compatibility with a broad range of quantum hardware backends and simulation platforms. Drawing on the reasoning provided by the denotational semantics of quantum subroutines, this work also highlights the key distinctions between quantum unit testing and its classical counterpart.

papers.title: On the hardness of approximating minimum distances of quantum codes
papers.summary: The problem of computing distances of error-correcting codes is fundamental in both the classical and quantum settings. While hardness for the classical version of these problems has been known for some time (in both the exact and approximate settings), it was only recently that Kapshikar and Kundu showed the hardness of these problems for non-degenerate quantum codes. As our first main result, we get a direct reduction to CSS codes, the most commonly used type of quantum code, from the minimum distance problem for classical linear codes. In particular, our proof uses arguably simpler constructions based on hypergraph product codes. Our second set of results considers the distance of a graph state, which is a key parameter for quantum codes obtained via the codeword stabilized formalism. We show that it is NP-hard to compute/approximate the distance of a graph state, which is a degenerate quantum code, when the adjacency matrix of the graph is the input. This establishes hardness for even degenerate quantum codes, which was not known before. Furthermore, we show this is true even if we only consider X-type errors of a graph state. Our techniques, moreover, imply an interesting classical consequence: the hardness of computing or approximating the distance of classical codes with rate equal to 1/2. One of the main motivations of the present work is a question raised by Kapshikar and Kundu concerning the NP-hardness of approximation when there is an additive error proportional to a quantum code's length. We show that no such hardness can hold for hypergraph product codes. These observations suggest the possibility of a new kind of square root barrier.

papers.title: Mitigating the barren plateau problem in linear optics
papers.summary: We prove that variational quantum algorithms using discrete variable boson samplers suffer from barren plateaus and that by changing to fermionic statistics, which is classically efficient to simulate, the barren plateau scaling is less severe. Moreover, when using fermionic statistics the cost landscape boils down to one unit frequency Fourier mode per variational parameter, irrespective of circuit design, ansatz or variational problem, allowing for more efficient parameter shift rules. This simplified cost landscape allows for the gradient-free Rotosolve algorithm to be used to gain a considerable speed-up over the original bosonic algorithm. Motivated by this, we propose a non-linear parametrised phase shifter, the dual-valued phase shifter, that generates these single-harmonic cost landscapes for bosonic statistics. We propose three ways to achieve this by using either non-linear optics, measurement-induced non-linearities, or entangled resource states simulating fermionic statistics. The latter two require linear optics only, allowing for implementation with widely-available technology today. Despite this, the classical simulability of free fermions and the fact the fermionic algorithm can defeat the bosonic algorithm casts doubt on whether the quantum advantage of boson sampling results in any practical advantage in this setting.

papers.title: Temporal entanglement transition in chaotic quantum many-body dynamics
papers.summary: Temporal entanglement (TE) of an influence matrix (IM) has been proposed as a measure of complexity of simulating dynamics of local observables in a many-body system. Foligno et al. [Phys. Rev. X 13, 041008 (2023)] recently argued that the TE in chaotic 1d quantum circuits obeys linear (volume-law) scaling with evolution time. To reconcile this apparent high complexity of IM with the rapid thermalization of local observables, here we study the relation between TE, non-Markovianity, and local temporal correlations for chaotic quantum baths. By exactly solving a random-unitary bath model, and bounding distillable entanglement between future and past degrees of freedom, we identify a regime where TE is extensive and reflects genuine non-Markovianity. This memory, however, is entirely contained in highly complex temporal correlations, and its effect on few-point temporal correlators is negligible. An IM coarse-graining procedure, reducing the allowed frequency of measurements of the probe system, results in a transition from volume- to {subvolume- (area or logarithmic)} law TE scaling. We demonstrate the generality of this TE transition in 1d circuits by analyzing the kicked Ising model analytically at dual-unitary points, as well as numerically away from them. This finding indicates that dynamics of local observables are fully captured by a subvolume-law IM. We provide evidence that the compact IM MPS obtained via standard compression algorithms accurately describes local~evolution.

papers.title: A General Framework for Constructing Local Hidden-state Models to Determine the Steerability
papers.summary: Not all entangled states can exhibit quantum steering, and determining whether a given entangled state is steerable is a crucial problem in quantum information theory. The main challenge lies in verifying the existence of a local hidden-state (LHS) model capable of reproducing all post-measurement assemblages generated by arbitrary measurements. To address this, we propose a machine learning-based framework that employs batch sampling of measurements and gradient-based optimization to construct an optimal LHS model. We validate our method by analyzing the steerability of two-qubit Werner and two-qutrit isotropic states. For Werner states, our approach saturates the analytical visibility bounds under three Pauli measurements, arbitrary projective measurements (PVMs), and arbitrary positive operator-valued measurements (POVMs). For isotropic states, we achieve the known analytical bounds under arbitrary PVMs. We further investigate the steerability of this class of states under arbitrary POVMs, and our results suggest that POVMs can offer an advantage over PVMs in revealing the steerability of such states.

papers.title: Tensor computing application programming interface: An application-oriented, lightweight API for portable high-performance tensor network computations
papers.summary: Tensor networks (TNs) are a central computational tool in quantum science and artificial intelligence. However, the lack of a unified software interface across tensor-computing frameworks severely limits the portability of TN applications, coupling algorithmic development to specific hardware and software back ends. To address this challenge, we introduce the Tensor Computing Application Programming Interface (TCAPI)---an application-oriented, lightweight API designed to enable framework-independent, high-performance TN applications, currently specified for \texttt{C++} and \texttt{Python}. TCAPI provides well-defined type-system conventions that abstract tensor objects, together with a minimal yet expressive set of core functions for essential tensor manipulations and tensor linear-algebra operations, with operation semantics shared across language specifications. Through numerical demonstrations of representative tensor-network applications implemented in \texttt{C++} using TCAPI, we show that code written against TCAPI can be migrated seamlessly across heterogeneous hardware and software platforms while achieving performance comparable to native framework implementations. We further provide open-source implementations of TCAPI based on \textit{Cytnx} and \textit{ITensor} in \texttt{C++}, and on \textit{NumPy} in \texttt{Python}, demonstrating its practicality and ease of integration with existing tensor-computing frameworks.

papers.title: Multipath wave-particle duality with exact quantification of which-path knowledge
papers.summary: A quantum system (quanton) traverses an interferometer with $N$ equally probable paths and interacts with another quantum system (detector) that stores path information in a set of symmetric states. In this framework, we present a systematic quantitative study of wave-particle duality based on entropic trade-off relations between quantum coherence, characterized by the relative entropy of coherence of the quanton state, and which-path knowledge, quantified by the mutual information obtained through detector-state discrimination. Unlike prior upper-bound-based formulations, we obtain an exact quantification of which-path knowledge for the discrimination strategies considered here, encompassing previous strategies and extending beyond them. A general optimal measurement is implemented through a state-separation map governed by a continuous parameter $\xi\in[0,1]$, followed by minimum-error (ME) discrimination of either the successful outputs only (standard approach) or both successful and failure outputs (concatenated approach). Our framework identifies a strategy-dependent hierarchy that generally emerges in the tightness of the resulting duality relations. At $\xi=0$, both approaches reduce to the ME measurement, which typically yields the tightest relation. For $\xi>0$, each approach yields a distinct relation that generally becomes less tight as $\xi$ increases, with the concatenated strategy always yielding a relation at least as tight as its standard counterpart. We further characterize saturation of these relations by identifying the detector-state sets that lead to it and show that nontrivial saturation occurs only for interferometers with a nonprime number of paths. From these sets, we elucidate how the underlying structure of the quanton-detector correlations gives rise to this behavior and explains the lack of universal saturation in multipath duality relations for pure states.

papers.title: A Route to Quantum-Coherent Thermodynamics
papers.summary: Equilibrium thermodynamics emerges because a vast number of microscopic states become indistinguishable at the level of local observables. We start from the observation that a nonequilibrium quantum state can also be represented by an ensemble of pure states that minimizes the average energy variance. We show that varying the statistical weights within this optimal family organizes state space into ``minimum-variance leaves'', which generalize the space of stationary states underlying equilibrium. We observe thermodynamic compression on the leaves, which in the simplest scenario manifests itself in the indistinguishability of states with the same energy density. We call this ``leaf typicality''; at equilibrium it reduces to eigenstate thermalization or its generalizations. Numerical tests support leaf typicality on some leaves and indicate a breakdown of its stronger forms on others, suggesting a rich thermodynamic organization beyond equilibrium. These results open a route to a unified statistical mechanics of equilibrium and nonequilibrium quantum states.

papers.title: Tight Quantum Speed Limit for Ergotropy Charging in the N-Qubit Dicke Battery
papers.summary: We derive a quantum speed limit for ergotropy charging in the $N$-qubit Dicke battery. With the qubits initially in their ground state and the charger in a coherent state of mean photon number $\bar{n}$, the charging time to a target fraction $\varepsilon$ of the maximum extractable work obeys, in the classical-field limit, $\Gamma_N \tau^{*}(\varepsilon) \geq \arcsin\sqrt{\varepsilon}$, where $\Gamma_N = 2\lambda\sqrt{\bar{n}/N}$ is a single rate combining the light-matter coupling, the charger amplitude and the system size. The bound is geometric: although the ergotropy is defined by an optimisation over unitaries, it reduces to a fixed function of the angle swept by the collective spin on the Bloch sphere, and the drive bounds the rate at which that angle can grow, so the charging time is at least the required arc divided by the maximum angular velocity. The reduction rests on an exact statement about work extraction: only the coherent component of the drive delivers extractable work, while its vacuum fluctuations deposit energy that remains locked in the passive state. This makes the short-time coefficient independent of the charger occupation, and it is what separates a bound on extractable work from a bound on stored energy, which no instantaneous-power argument can supply. At finite charger occupation the inequality is tested rather than proved: numerical integration of the full Dicke Hamiltonian, with a dynamical charger and a mixed battery state, finds the bound respected at every admitted charging time for two to five qubits, and approached most closely in the limit of small target work. The familiar square-root estimate is the chord to this arc, recovered in the small-angle limit and weaker whenever a large fraction of the maximum work is required.

papers.title: Deterministic feedforward-based generation of large optical coherent-state superposition
papers.summary: Large optical coherent-state superpositions are essential to advance quantum sensing, quantum repeaters and error-correction codes. We propose a deterministic feedforward protocol employing qubit-mode dispersive coupling, currently available in cavity quantum electrodynamics (QED). We show this single-mode protocol to outperform the advanced three-mode Gaussian-photon-number-resolving detector scheme both in terms of average fidelity and quantum non-Gaussian phase-space properties, and propose sensitivity to weak displacements of interference fringes as a feasible and conclusive witness of quantum interference. This approach combining QED with electro-optical feedforward is extendable to tailored states for applications and other platforms.

papers.title: Quantum Algorithms for Gibbs Expectation of Non-log-concave and Heavy-tailed Distributions
papers.summary: We establish a systematic framework of unbiased quantum sampling and estimation protocols for the classical Gibbs expectation. This framework generalizes existing approaches to the partition function estimation and has broader applications in various fields. We consider sampling and estimation for a wide class of non-log-concave distributions, particularly heavy-tailed ones, under relaxed assumptions beyond strong convexity, such as dissipativity. We develop an unbiased extension of quantum-accelerated multilevel Monte Carlo (QA-MLMC) to eliminate all biases from discretization and time truncation, together with introducing a change-of-measure approach and the Girsanov theorem via Radon-Nikodym derivatives. As a result, our approach achieves quantum complexity $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-1})$ within error $\epsilon$, whereas the classical MLMC requires $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2})$ and existing quantum algorithms yield biased estimators under stronger assumptions. Furthermore, our unified framework enables unbiased quantum sampling and estimation for certain heavy-tailed distributions after transformation. We provide several concrete applications of our approach in statistics, machine learning, and finance, towards more practical scenarios of the quantum acceleration of stochastic processes.

papers.title: Scalable Determination of Penalization Weights for Constrained Optimizations on Approximate Solvers
papers.summary: Quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) provides problem formulations for various computational problems that can be solved with dedicated QUBO solvers, based on classical or quantum computation. A common approach to constrained combinatorial optimization problems is to enforce the constraints in the QUBO formulation by adding penalization terms. Penalization introduces an additional hyperparameter that significantly affects the solver's efficacy: the relative weight between the objective terms and the penalization terms. Here we study the problem of a priori determining suitable penalization weights from a foundational and practical perspective. We formally establish that finding its optimal value for Gibbs solvers is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard even approximately and $\#\mathsf{P}$-hard exactly. This serves us as a motivation to develop a widely applicable heuristic strategy for determining suitable penalization weights, with provable guarantees for Gibbs solvers, and polynomial complexity for broad problem classes. Experiments across diverse problems and solver architectures, including large-scale instances on Fujitsu's Digital Annealer, show robust performance and order-of-magnitude speedups over existing heuristics. We further extend the strategy to quantum approximate optimization and demonstrate its performance on Quantinuum's H2-2 trapped-ion processor.

papers.title: One pure steered state implies Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen steering for two-qubit entangled states
papers.summary: In this work, we show that a two-qubit entangled state admitting at least one pure steered state is Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) steerable from Alice to Bob. Pure steered states signifies that the quantum steering ellipsoid of Bob is tangent to his Bloch sphere at least at a single point. Furthermore, we prove that for a two-qubit entangled state, Bob's quantum steering ellipsoid is tangent to his Bloch sphere at exactly $N$ points, for $N\in \{ 0,1,2,\infty\}$, if and only if Alice's quantum steering ellipsoid is tangent to her Bloch sphere at exactly $N$ points. For any two-qubit entangled state, therefore, if one party can steer the other to at least one pure state, the state is two-way EPR steerable. We also present several illuminating examples of two-qubit entangled states such that the EPR steering can be verified in terms of pure steered states. Our result addresses the Gisin theorem in a EPR steering scenario: at least a single pure steered state implies two-way steering.

papers.title: On Performance and Limitations of Quantum Wave Packet Dynamics Simulated using NISQ Hardware
papers.summary: We investigate one-dimensional quantum wave-packet dynamics using a grid-based encoding of the wave function onto qubit registers. Time evolution is implemented using a split operator approach, with the kinetic energy operator realized via the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and arbitrary discretized potentials represented by commuting Pauli-Z gates. The algorithm is benchmarked against classical grid-based simulations and validated using a noiseless Qiskit Statevector simulator before being implemented on current quantum hardware (IBM Quantum and IonQ) for qubit counts ranging from two to five. Good agreement with benchmark calculations is obtained for two- and three-qubit implementations, while deviations increase at larger qubit counts due to hardware noise and increased circuit depth. Among the devices examined, the algorithm maintains closer agreement with the benchmark on the trapped-ion IonQ Forte processor as the number of qubits increases.

papers.title: Geometric Construction of Optimal Teleportation Witnesses
papers.summary: Not all entangled states are useful for quantum teleportation. We present a geometric method to construct optimal teleportation witnesses, which provide operational necessary and sufficient criteria for identifying the teleportation usefulness of arbitrary two-qudit entangled states. Specifically, by developing a two-layer iterative cutting-plane algorithm to solve the shortest distance problem from the target state $\rho$ to the convex set $S$ of useless states, we obtain the projection point $\sigma^* \in S$ and then construct the optimal teleportation witness from the projection geometry. Moreover, the shortest distance $D(\rho)$ obtained during this construction also serves as a necessary and sufficient criterion for usefulness. We apply our method to identify the teleportation usefulness of three classes of entangled states.

papers.title: QML-PipeGuard: Detecting Channel-Substitution Attacks on Quantum Machine Learning Pipelines in Untrusted Clouds
papers.summary: As machine-learning workloads move onto quantum hardware they inherit a trust problem classical AI deployments have largely solved and quantum ones have not: quantum machine learning (QML) is already sold as a cloud service, and a customer cannot check that the circuit they paid for is actually the circuit that ran. We show the gap is exploitable. A malicious or cost-cutting provider can substitute the declared quantum channel with one that reproduces every accuracy test the customer performs, passes the single-observable checks used in practice, and still differs from the declared computation at the channel level. We call this a channel-substitution attack and instantiate it in three deployments: audit evasion, service downgrade, and result forgery in reproducibility review. QML-PipeGuard detects the attack at runtime from measurement statistics the customer already collects. Its guarantee is two-sided, stated in the distance a local verifier measures: any substitution shifting a single-qubit output marginal by $\delta$ in trace norm forces a contract deviation of at least $\delta/\sqrt{3}$, the constant tight and independent of qubit count; the guarantee is relative to the chosen observable family and reference-input set. For local-unitary substitutions the adversary's blind set is characterised exactly, as a commutation condition, which gives the defender a rule for choosing challenge inputs that shrinks it. A finite-shot budget rule bounds false accepts and false alarms at once, one tolerance separates attack from the benign drift observed here, and every decision enters a hash-anchored audit trail. On an IBM Heron r2 processor a substituted quantum-kernel intrusion-detection pipeline evades the weak contract and our verifier halts it, while the honest channel stays within tolerance.

papers.title: Continuous-time quantum control across an exponentially small bottleneck in a frustrated Ising ring model
papers.summary: Continuous-time Quantum Annealing (QA) is a strategy for preparing the ground state of nontrivial many-body systems. In its standard form, the dynamics is generated by a time-dependent interpolation between a simple driving Hamiltonian and the target problem Hamiltonian, usually implemented through a linear schedule. This approach faces the crucial bottleneck of small spectral gaps, which may require exponentially long annealing times to ensure adiabaticity. Here, we show how to implement quantum control over the annealing schedule in a frustrated Ising ring, one of the simplest models exhibiting an exponentially small bottleneck gap. By optimizing smooth continuous-time annealing schedules with a dressed-CRAB approach, and using a digitized representation of the dynamics to efficiently evaluate gradients, we construct protocols that strongly outperform standard fixed schedules. The optimized dynamics bypasses the bottleneck through a strongly nonadiabatic mechanism, leading to efficient ground-state preparation despite the exponentially small minimum gap. In particular, the annealing time required to reach a fixed residual-energy threshold is found to grow linearly with system size rather than exponentially. We further examine a lowest-order variational counter-diabatic correction and find that, once schedule optimization is allowed, it does not lead to any improvement.

papers.title: Complete Relational Description of Spin in a Quantum Background
papers.summary: The standard description of the state of a spin in quantum mechanics presupposes externally fixed directions -- a classical background. Can a spin be fully described instead in relation to other quantum mechanical systems? Poulin suggested twenty years ago group averaging over rotations the joint state of a fundamental spin and a reference spin with large angular momentum which, however, yields a classical bit in a probabilistic mixture. We revisit this idea and show that when the quantum reference system is augmented to \emph{two} large spins, the standard quantum mechanical description of a spin is recovered in the limit of large quantum numbers for the reference system.

papers.title: Higher-Order Magnus Corrections to Leakage Elimination Operator-Based Quantum Control Pulse Design in the Low-Frequency Regime
papers.summary: Effective quantum control is essential for quantum computing and information processing, yet level leakage remains a bottleneck limiting control fidelity. The leakage elimination operator (LEO) approach is highly effective at suppressing leakage from a target subspace to other subspaces. Analytical control conditions under the high-frequency driving limit have been derived via the Feshbach PQ partitioning technique. However, the driving intensity is subject to fundamental physical bounds, and low-frequency driving is experimentally more feasible. In this work, we reformulate LEO within the Magnus framework and extend it beyond the high-frequency limit. We show that the analytical control conditions obtained from the Feshbach PQ partitioning technique are equivalent to the zeroth-order Magnus expansion. We then analyze the higher-order Magnus corrections. By minimizing the leakage, we obtain a modified pulse condition suitable for the low-frequency regime. As an illustrative example, we study near-perfect state transfer through a one-dimensional spin chain under LEO control. We find that the second-order Magnus correction improves the transmission fidelity at low-frequency driving, while the improvement becomes negligible at high frequencies. Our results provide an effective route for designing control pulses in the low-frequency regime, with potential applications in superconducting qubits, trapped ions, and solid-state spin systems.

papers.title: Temperature Beyond Equilibrium in Isolated Quantum Many-Body Systems and Their Subsystems
papers.summary: Temperature is one of the central concepts of thermodynamics, yet its meaning far from equilibrium remains unclear. The problem is especially challenging in isolated quantum many-body systems, whose states evolve unitarily, may remain far from equilibrium, and retain energy coherence, a genuinely quantum feature with no direct classical counterpart. Specifically, energy fluctuations in a nonstationary quantum state have two distinct origins. Part of these fluctuations comes from uncertainty in the energy populations and has the usual thermodynamic meaning. The rest comes from quantum coherence between energy sectors and is responsible for the state's time dependence. We propose that, even away from equilibrium, temperature identifies the state within the family of regular states sharing the same energy-coherence structure. The resulting inverse temperature is obtained from a principle of minimum discrimination information, which selects the least distinguishable state compatible with the prescribed energy and coherence structure. This replaces the usual maximum-entropy principle, which, applied naively, can yield a biased estimator of the inverse temperature. We also lay the groundwork for an extension of the construction to subsystems and show that, although the inverse temperature of a subsystem is not determined by its reduced state alone, under an alignment assumption, its instantaneous rate of change is a local quantity for sufficiently large subsystems.

papers.title: Proof-of-Principle Implementation of Quantum Key Distribution in an Indefinite Causal Order
papers.summary: In quantum physics, the order in which different operations occur can be placed in superposition. The resulting processes have an indefinite causal order, which is of fundamental interest and can be viewed as a novel quantum resource enabling new protocols. Here, we report an experimental proof-of-principle implementation of one such protocol, where we perform BB84-like quantum cryptography by placing \AB's measurement-and-preparation operations in a photonic quantum SWITCH. By embedding \AB\ within the quantum SWITCH, the protocol achieves an average eavesdropper detection probability of $0.15 \pm 0.02$ per shared qubit, with eavesdropper detection performed through measurements of the control qubit rather than comparing the key. Unlike standard BB84 and related schemes, which detect eavesdropping by publicly revealing and discarding a fraction of the raw key, our approach requires no disclosure of key material: every retained qubit can, in principle, be tested for eavesdropping while remaining available for key generation. Although the present implementation does not yet constitute a secure quantum key distribution protocol, owing to post-selection required for measurements within the quantum SWITCH, it provides a proof of principle that indefinite causal order can be exploited to detect eavesdropping without sacrificing key bits.
